desc:
In one operation you may replace any single character of the string s with any lowercase letter. Turn s into a palindrome using the fewest operations. If several palindromes can be reached with that fewest number of operations, return the lexicographically smallest of them.

For example, "egcfe" needs one operation (the mismatching pair is g and f), and writing the smaller letter gives "efcfe". "abcd" needs two operations and gives "abba". "racecars" gives "raaccaar".
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Which characters of the string are forced to be equal in any palindrome?
Position i and position n - 1 - i form a pair that must end up equal. Different pairs do not influence each other.
For a mismatching pair one replacement is enough and it must overwrite one side with the other letter. To get the smallest result, overwrite the larger letter with the smaller one.
editorial: Split the string into independent pairs (s[i], s[n-1-i]) with i < n - 1 - i; the middle letter of an odd-length string is free. A pair that already matches costs nothing. A mismatching pair needs at least one replacement, and exactly one is enough: copy one letter over the other.

That fixes the minimum number of operations, and it also limits the choices: for a mismatching pair, the final common letter must be one of the two existing letters. Choosing the smaller one makes the string as small as possible, and the choices for different pairs are independent, so the greedy per-pair choice is globally smallest.
Implementation: walk two pointers inwards, write the minimum of the two letters at both places. Time O(n), space O(n) for the output.
